passage: Your chechi Binita was fifteen when she got that photo app, mone. Your grandpa Jomon watched it all. Every night she would lie on the sofa scrolling other girls' holidays and perfect skin, and her face would go flat. If a photo got fewer hearts than her friend's, she deleted it. One evening she said, "Appachan, everyone's life is better than mine." I didn't lecture her. I just asked her to help with the church choir's Christmas concert, since she sings well. She came to practice every week. On the night she sang the solo, and her school friends came and shouted her name. After that I noticed she scrolled less. She'd say, "Can't, practice."

qa.q: What would Binita do if a photo got fewer hearts than her friend's?
qa.a: She deleted it.

qa.q: What does Binita's flat face while scrolling suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt low and behind, comparing herself with other girls' holidays and perfect skin.

qa.q: What turning point did the choir concert bring?
qa.a: Singing the solo with her real friends cheering gave her worth she could feel offline, and after that she scrolled less.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Binita said everyone's life was better than hers?
qa.a: He was probably worried and sad, which is why he looked for something real she could shine at instead of lecturing.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a fifteen-year-old whose mood rose and fell with likes, and how singing with friends gave her firmer ground.

passage: The school trek to Kalsubai had one bar of signal, Omkar's battery was at nine percent, and he was panicking. He'd posted a gym photo that morning and it had only fourteen likes. Aparna's post had two hundred. "Everyone thinks I'm a joke," he muttered, holding the phone up to the grey sky. "Your phone's going to die anyway," Aparna said, pulling up her hood. "Help me with the tent?" The phone died at the second pole. They got the tent up in the drizzle, badly, then properly, laughing when it collapsed on Aparna. That night by the lantern, their teacher said theirs was the best-pitched tent in the group. Omkar realised he hadn't thought about the likes in hours.

qa.q: How many likes did Omkar's gym photo get?
qa.a: It got fourteen likes.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he held the phone up to the sky, and why?
qa.a: He felt anxious and embarrassed, thinking everyone saw him as a joke because his post had fewer likes than Aparna's.

qa.q: What turning point came once the phone died?
qa.a: He joined Aparna in pitching the tent, and the shared effort and the teacher's praise gave him firmer ground than likes.

qa.q: How might Aparna have seen Omkar's worry about likes?
qa.a: She seemed to see it as less important than what was in front of them, and gently pulled him into doing something together.

grounding: On a trek with a dying phone, a teenager who measures himself by likes finds firmer ground in a shared task and a friend.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m. Posted the photo from Irawati's party at seven. Forty-one likes. Irawati's got three hundred in an hour. I've checked it about fifty times. Deleted it at ten, because forty-one looked pathetic next to hers. Scrolled through everyone's holidays: Irawati in the hills, two seniors at some beach, and me in this room with a leaking tap. I feel so behind I could scream. But today, before all that, I fixed Dadi's radio with a screwdriver, and she clapped like I'd won something. That felt better than any like. Maybe tomorrow I'll leave the phone in the kitchen and finish the cycle repair with Chacha.
Lokesh

qa.q: How many likes did Lokesh's photo get?
qa.a: Forty-one likes.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel scrolling through everyone's holidays?
qa.a: Lokesh felt behind and frustrated, measuring life against others' posts.

qa.q: What gives Lokesh firmer ground than likes?
qa.a: Real things like fixing Dadi's radio and repairing the cycle with Chacha.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when the radio worked again?
qa.a: Dadi was delighted and proud, clapping as if Lokesh had won something.

grounding: Shows a teen whose self-worth rises and falls with likes, finding firmer ground in offline achievement.

passage: In the kasba near Satara, the network was only strong on the roof of the post office, so Madhuri climbed up there every evening to scroll. Girls from Mumbai with perfect skin, cafés and trips abroad. Her own face, in the phone's camera, looked dull and dusty. She had started asking her cousin Madhav, "Do I look too village?" before every photo. Last Saturday her picture of the temple fair got only nine likes, and she skipped dinner. But on Sunday, at the district relay, she ran the last leg and pulled her team from third to first. Madhav lifted her onto his shoulders. The whole kasba cheered. That evening she didn't climb the post office roof at all.

qa.q: Where was the network strong in the kasba?
qa.a: On the roof of the post office.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel about herself while scrolling?
qa.a: She felt dull and behind, comparing her face and life to girls from Mumbai.

qa.q: What gave Madhuri firmer ground than likes?
qa.a: Running the last leg at the district relay and winning with her team.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt lifting Madhuri onto his shoulders?
qa.a: Madhav was likely proud and happy for her, sharing in the win.

grounding: Shows a teen measuring herself against curated images and likes, finding firmer ground in an offline achievement.

passage:
At midnight in his room in Mexico City, Alejandro was still scrolling a photo app. Boys his age on beaches, with sharp jawlines and hundreds of likes. His own post from the morning had eleven. He deleted it.
He checked again at breakfast. Nothing new. His chest felt heavy all day.
On Saturday his friend Kofi turned up with a bag of spanners. "The bike, remember? You promised."
They spent the afternoon fixing the old bicycle in the courtyard, hands black with grease. Kofi's little brother cheered when the chain finally caught.
That evening Alejandro rode it round the block twice. He didn't take a single photo. He noticed, falling asleep, that he hadn't opened the app all day, and that the day had felt good anyway.

qa.q: How many likes did Alejandro's morning post have?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Alejandro feel after deleting his post?
qa.a: He felt behind and low; his chest felt heavy all day and he kept checking for likes.

qa.q: What gave Alejandro firmer ground than likes?
qa.a: Fixing the bike with Kofi and riding it gave him a real achievement and friendship, which felt good without being posted.

qa.q: How might Kofi see that Saturday?
qa.a: To Kofi it was just keeping a promise and having fun fixing the bike; he may not know how much the afternoon lifted Alejandro.

grounding: Shows a teen whose self-worth rises and falls with likes finding firmer ground in an offline project with a friend.
